title: The Titanic Graves of Halifax
summary: The Nova Scotia city where ships brought 209 bodies from the Titanic disaster in 1912 - burying 150 of them in three cemeteries, including the probable inspiration for James Cameron's 'Jack Dawson.'

content.intro: When the RMS Titanic sank 400 miles southeast of Newfoundland on April 15, 1912, the nearest major port was Halifax, Nova Scotia. The cable ship Mackay-Bennett was dispatched with embalming supplies, coffins, and clergy to recover bodies from the freezing Atlantic. Over three weeks, ships brought 209 bodies to Halifax. Some were claimed by wealthy families and shipped elsewhere. But 150 remain buried in three Halifax cemeteries - the largest collection of Titanic victims anywhere. The graves range from elaborate monuments to simple numbered markers for the unidentified. One stone reads 'J. Dawson' - not Leonardo DiCaprio's character, but Joseph Dawson, a coal trimmer. When James Cameron discovered this grave while filming, he was startled; he claims he didn't know a J. Dawson had actually died on the Titanic when he named his fictional hero.

sections.title: The Recovery
sections.body: Halifax was the obvious choice for a grim task. It was the closest major port with cable ships capable of extended ocean work. The Mackay-Bennett departed April 17 carrying ice, coffins, and embalming supplies. It reached the debris field on April 20 and found bodies floating in life jackets, preserved by the near-freezing water. Over the next week, crews recovered 306 bodies. Space limitations forced terrible decisions: first-class passengers were embalmed and coffined; crew and steerage were preserved in canvas or, when supplies ran out, buried at sea. The ship returned to Halifax on April 30. Other vessels followed; ultimately 333 bodies were recovered, and 209 were brought to Halifax.

sections.title: The Burials
sections.body: Halifax undertakers worked around the clock to prepare bodies for identification and burial. Families claimed some; 59 were shipped elsewhere. But 150 remained. They were buried in three cemeteries based on religion: Fairview Lawn Cemetery (Protestant), Mount Olivet Cemetery (Catholic), and Baron de Hirsch Cemetery (Jewish). Some had names; some had only numbers. Marker 227 reads simply 'Unknown.' The arrangement at Fairview Lawn is striking - rows of black granite headstones curving slightly, representing (some say) the curve of a ship's hull. It's probably coincidental, but the effect is powerful.

sections.title: The Unknown Child
sections.body: One of the most visited graves belongs to an unknown child, originally marked simply '4.' For decades, the child's identity was a mystery that haunted Halifax. Forensic science eventually provided answers - and more questions. DNA testing identified him as Sidney Leslie Goodwin, a 19-month-old from England emigrating with his family; all eight Goodwins died. But earlier testing had identified a different child; the case remains somewhat contested. The grave marker, now replaced with one reading 'The Unknown Child,' is covered in toys, coins, and flowers. Visitors still leave offerings for the anonymous victim who represented all the children lost.

sections.title: J. Dawson
sections.body: Near the end of a row at Fairview Lawn lies stone 227: 'J. Dawson, Died April 15, 1912, SS Titanic.' This was Joseph Dawson, a 23-year-old Irish coal trimmer from Dublin - one of the 'black gang' who shoveled coal in the ship's boilers. He was a real person who died a real death. When James Cameron's 1997 film featured a fictional hero named Jack Dawson, fans converged on the grave. Cameron claims he didn't know a J. Dawson had existed when he wrote the screenplay; he chose the name because it was common. The grave now receives more visitors than any other, many leaving roses and movie ticket stubs.

sections.title: Visiting the Titanic Cemeteries
sections.body: Fairview Lawn Cemetery, at 3720 Windsor Street in Halifax, holds 121 Titanic victims and is the most visited. Mount Olivet Cemetery (on Mumford Road) holds 19 Catholic victims. Baron de Hirsch Cemetery (on Cornwallis Street) holds 10 Jewish victims. All three are open to visitors during daylight hours. The Maritime Museum of the Atlantic downtown houses the largest Titanic artifact collection outside Belfast and the wreck itself - including a deckchair, shoes, and the Titanic's only recovered wooden fragment. Grave locations are mapped at each cemetery entrance. Halifax Stanfield International Airport is 23 miles north. The cemeteries are accessible by Halifax Transit.

content.flightContext: Located at 44.65°N, 63.60°W in Halifax, Nova Scotia. From altitude, Fairview Lawn Cemetery appears as a large green space in Halifax's north end. The curved rows of Titanic graves are visible as a distinct section if conditions allow. Downtown Halifax and the harbor are to the southeast. The Maritime Museum is on the waterfront. Halifax Harbor, where the recovery ships docked, opens to the Atlantic. Halifax Stanfield International Airport is 23 miles north. The city's role in the Titanic story reflects its position as the major North Atlantic port closest to the disaster site.
